title: Mercy
synopsis: An AI judge promised perfect justice. You're the defense attorney for a client it just decided is guilty. You have twenty-four hours to convince a machine of something it doesn't have a word for.

nodes.text: MERCY returns in 0.4 seconds. There is no gavel; there is a chime, and then a PDF. Your client — seventeen, undocumented, five foot one in shoes she borrowed for court — is guilty at 96.8% confidence, printed in the same font as everything else on the page. Sentencing is tomorrow at nine. You have until then to write an appeal that will be read by nothing with a face.

choices.text: Read the model card immediately
choices.consequence: You go at the machine before you go to the girl, because the machine has documentation and the girl has hope. You will feel that ordering later.

choices.text: Call your client first
choices.consequence: You call the holding facility before reading a page, and Sara answers already crying. Twenty minutes out of twenty-four hours, and you would spend them again.

nodes.text: Twelve hundred pages, and the interesting sentence sits on page nine hundred and four, in a footnote, in a smaller point size: 'a measured bias floor of 1.4% on minority defendants, within acceptable bounds.' Acceptable to whom is not specified. You do the arithmetic anyway. Fourteen thousand cases a year run through MERCY in this state. One point four percent isn't a rounding error. It's a small town.

choices.text: Focus the appeal on the bias floor
choices.consequence: You aim at the machine instead of the case, which is either the biggest swing of your career or malpractice, depending entirely on Thursday.

choices.text: Focus on your specific client's case
choices.consequence: You put the footnote in a drawer and go back to one girl and one night. Winning small is still winning, and Sara doesn't get to appeal twice.

nodes.text: Sara hasn't slept in thirty-one hours and keeps apologizing for how she looks on the video link. She didn't do it. She also didn't not-do-it in any format the training set recognizes: her alibi is her aunt's church, in Mam, a congregation with no digital footprint and eight members who will not file affidavits with anyone in a uniform. Truth exists here. It simply isn't machine-readable.

choices.text: Promise her you'll win
choices.consequence: You say the word 'promise' to a seventeen-year-old about something you cannot control. It buys her four hours of sleep and costs you the rest of the night.

choices.text: Tell her the odds honestly
choices.consequence: You give her the real number and watch her take it better than most adults do. 'Okay,' she says. 'So what do we do at three percent?'

nodes.text: An email you sent to six former employees gets exactly one answer, at 3:14 in the morning, from an account with no name attached. She spent nineteen months on the calibration team. She'll meet you in person: no phones, no video, a diner off Route 9 she picks herself. She has a USB drive. The last line reads, 'I'm not brave. I'm just done being able to sleep.'

choices.text: Meet her at the diner she suggests
choices.consequence: You drive ninety minutes at four in the morning on a stranger's word. Every reasonable instinct says trap. You go anyway, and you leave your phone in the trunk.

choices.text: Ask for the file remotely first
choices.consequence: You ask her to upload it and she stops answering for six hours. Caution is free until it isn't, and you just spent a quarter of your day learning that.

nodes.text: Adams has been a prosecutor twenty-two years and a believer for two. He buys the coffee and explains, without heat, that he has watched judges sentence by hunger, by tee time, by what a defendant's father did in 1988. MERCY doesn't do that. MERCY has never once been late for lunch. He is not, in the way that matters, wrong about the thing he is comparing it to.

choices.text: Try to flip him on this specific case
choices.consequence: You work the one case instead of the philosophy, because he can concede a girl without conceding a religion. He agrees to read a single file.

choices.text: Plan to outflank him
choices.consequence: You decide he can't be moved and start building around him. It is the correct tactical read, and you will spend a year regretting it.

nodes.text: The drive holds the internal audits nobody filed with the state. Sixty-one percent of the training incidents come from four census tracts. The 'high-risk associate' tags — the feature that weighed hardest against Sara — were hand-labeled by contractors at nineteen dollars an hour, working from social media, with an inter-rater agreement of 0.51. Half the model's moral authority was assembled by people who were guessing.

choices.text: Build the appeal around the data
choices.consequence: You spend the drive on one girl, which means the vendor gets it sealed afterward and nobody else ever sees a page of it. Sara first. Sara always.

choices.text: Save the data and use it for systemic suit
choices.consequence: You hold the best evidence you will ever own out of tomorrow's filing to protect a larger case. Sara is not told this. You don't sleep.

nodes.text: Marisol is fifteen and films everything, which is a personality defect right up until it becomes an alibi. On her phone: Sara, eating shaved ice, six miles from the scene, timestamped nine minutes before it happened, a bus rolling through frame with a route number you can verify. MERCY logged the submission and flagged it 'unverified, user-generated.' It never assigned the footage any weight at all.

choices.text: Get the video verified by a forensic lab
choices.consequence: You pay a lab out of your own account for a rush certification you cannot bill. Nine hours and eight hundred dollars to make a machine admit that a bus exists.

choices.text: Submit it to MERCY again with new metadata
choices.consequence: You resubmit with the transit authority's GPS log attached, teaching yourself the system's grammar in an afternoon. Confidence drops from 96.8 to 94.1. Not nearly enough.

nodes.text: The defense portal is a text field with a character counter and an evidence-packet uploader. No podium, no jury, nobody to look at while you say the thing. The counter runs grey to 8,000 and turns red after. You have written closings that made bailiffs look away, and tonight the most important paragraph of your life goes into a box that suggests, helpfully, that shorter submissions parse more reliably.

choices.text: Frame it as a procedural error
choices.consequence: You write it in the machine's language — evidentiary weighting, submission handling, remand for reprocessing. Cold, correct, and it never once says her name.

choices.text: Frame it as a story about Sara
choices.consequence: You write about the shaved ice and the borrowed shoes and the aunt's church, knowing the parser will discount every sentence. Somebody human might read it later.

nodes.text: There is exactly one person in Courtroom 4B with a pulse and authority: Judge Park, who signs off on MERCY's outputs at a rate of about ninety a day. She has read your filing. She is unimpressed by you and, you slowly understand, equally unimpressed by the terminal glowing at her left elbow. Then she asks a question that appears in no script: 'Counsel, who do you imagine I am in this room?'

choices.text: Argue to Park directly, off-script
choices.consequence: You close the binder and talk to her like a person, which is a procedural risk and the first honest thing said in that room all week.

choices.text: Submit through MERCY's official channels
choices.consequence: You take the safe route and file properly, and Park's face closes by a millimetre. You have just informed a judge that she is furniture.

nodes.text: A reporter from the state desk has the footnote — somebody leaked it, and it wasn't you. She files at six. Going loud puts 1.4% on a front page and puts a seventeen-year-old's arrest record beside it forever, along with her immigration status, her sister's face, and an address. Pressure is a tool. It is also a thing that lands on whoever happens to be standing underneath.

choices.text: Speak on record with Sara's permission
choices.consequence: You ask a minor to consent to being famous and she says yes in four seconds, which is precisely why you made yourself ask her twice.

choices.text: Decline; protect Sara's name
choices.consequence: You give the reporter nothing and lose the leverage that could have moved this in a day. Her family will never know what you turned down on their behalf.

nodes.text: He asks to meet somewhere that isn't the courthouse and shows up without a tie. He has read the audit twice, and it's the inter-rater number that got him. 'I sent forty people through that thing this year,' he says, and stops. Then: 'Prove it isn't an outlier. Give me a pattern I can put in a motion and I'll move to dismiss myself.' He means it, and that frightens him more than it frightens you.

choices.text: Promise him pattern evidence by tomorrow
choices.consequence: You promise a career prosecutor a statistical pattern in nineteen hours, with no analyst, no budget, and a paralegal who has a toddler at home.

choices.text: Push him to dismiss now
choices.consequence: You lean on a man already half-turned and watch him harden up again. Adams needed cover, not courage, and you just asked him for the wrong one.

nodes.text: Two in the morning, four people, one office, a printer that jams on page nine every time. The whistleblower makes coffee like it's a job she used to hold. Marisol is on the couch correcting MERCY's Mam translations line by line and getting angrier with each one. Your paralegal builds the exhibit index. You are dismantling something the state calls infallible with a legal pad and a stolen drive.

choices.text: Cut for clarity — three killer exhibits
choices.consequence: You throw out ninety pages at four in the morning and keep the bus, the tract map, and the 0.51. Anything a tired human can't hold in one hand loses.

choices.text: Submit everything — overwhelm the model
choices.consequence: You file all six hundred pages and let the parser drown in them. It isn't elegant. Neither is the thing you're arguing against.

nodes.text: She sends the clerk out and reads you three paragraphs from a document with no letterhead: her own report on MERCY's supervision regime, due to the judicial council in three weeks, currently unsigned. It uses the word 'unreviewable' four times. She has been on your side since before she met you. What she lacks is a case ugly enough to justify saying so out loud.

choices.text: Offer her this case as that cover
choices.consequence: You hand a judge the ammunition and the target in a single sentence. It is not improper. It is not entirely proper either, and you both know which.

choices.text: Promise her a cleaner case next month
choices.consequence: You offer to wait for a defendant with a cleaner record and a citizenship document. Park says nothing at all. Sara is sentenced at nine tomorrow regardless.

nodes.text: She wants to speak. MERCY takes no oral statements — the intake schema has no field for a voice — so anything she says enters as a transcript with a provenance flag that halves its weight. Putting her on that screen means a machine discounts her in real time while a room full of people watches it happen. She's seventeen. She has written it out on notebook paper, both sides.

choices.text: Let her speak; she has earned the room
choices.consequence: You let a girl read her own words into a system engineered to discount them, because Park is listening, and Park is not a system.

choices.text: Read her statement aloud for the record
choices.consequence: You read it in your own voice, which lands better and belongs to her less. She watches you do it and says nothing about it afterward.

nodes.text: The vendor sends a Palo Alto litigator with a beautiful suit and a genuinely warm handshake, and at 4:50 he files an emergency motion to seal the audit as trade secret. His brief runs forty pages and was clearly written before you ever found the drive. The clerk gives you until six to respond. One hour to explain why the arithmetic behind a conviction should not be somebody's intellectual property.

choices.text: Argue the public interest
choices.consequence: You write forty-one minutes of pure constitutional argument and none of it mentions Sara. The strongest brief you have ever filed, and it isn't hers.

choices.text: Negotiate a redacted release
choices.consequence: You trade away the vendor's names and internal emails to keep the numbers. Half a loaf — and the half you kept has a bus in it.

nodes.text: Nine in the morning. The terminal wakes with a soft chime somebody was paid to make reassuring. Park sits above everyone. Sara sits below everyone, in the borrowed shoes, her sister's hand flat against her back. Adams stands, clears his throat twice, and does not look at you. You stand. Everything you had, you spent. The room is very quiet for a place with no jury in it.

choices.text: Trust the work and let it play out
choices.consequence: You sit down and let the record be the record. It is the hardest professional act of your life and it takes about four seconds.

choices.text: Make one last argument from the heart
choices.consequence: You say something unbriefed about what a confidence interval cannot contain. The court reporter's hands stop for a moment, which is its own kind of verdict.

nodes.text: Park rules from the bench in ninety seconds: the audit is unsealed for the purposes of this proceeding, and the vendor may take it up on appeal. The litigator's warmth goes out like a pilot light. In the back row a reporter's phone starts buzzing and does not stop. Sara doesn't understand yet — she is reading faces, not words. Under the table you find her hand and hold it.

choices.text: Build the closing on the unsealed audit
choices.consequence: You rebuild the closing around numbers that are now permanently public. Sixty-one percent. Four tracts. 0.51. Let them live in a transcript forever.

choices.text: Move for immediate dismissal
choices.consequence: You go for the throat while the vendor's counsel is still pale. Speed over thoroughness, and you will spend a long time wondering about the trade.

nodes.text: Park reads it herself, aloud, on the record — she will not let the terminal print it. She vacates MERCY's finding, dismisses with prejudice, and refers the bias floor to the judicial council for inquiry. Then she takes off her glasses, which she has not done once in three days. The silence afterward feels less like victory than like a very old machine being handed back to people.

choices.text: Walk Sara out to her family
choices.consequence: You leave the paperwork on the table and walk a seventeen-year-old out through a door she had stopped picturing. The filing will still be there at four.

choices.text: File the systemic complaint today
choices.consequence: You stay in the emptying courtroom with a laptop while her family celebrates in the hallway. Momentum is a resource, and this one expires by Monday.

nodes.text: MERCY reviews the appeal, weighs it, and affirms itself at 94.4% — the machine cannot be embarrassed, which is the whole of its design. Park signs the order because she must, then attaches a concurrence so scathing that two law reviews reprint it entire. The appeal of the appeal takes two years and becomes the case that pulls MERCY out of three states. Sara serves fourteen months while that happens.

choices.text: Tell Sara what her case became
choices.consequence: You explain to a girl in a visiting room that her worst year became a citation. She asks whether it has helped anyone yet. You say: eventually.

choices.text: Keep her name out of every press hit
choices.consequence: You do forty interviews and never once say her name. The story gets smaller and she gets to have a life, and you take that trade without flinching.

nodes.text: MERCY is decommissioned and replaced by a hybrid: people deciding in front, models advising behind, every recommendation logged with the features that produced it. It is slower. It is inconsistent in exactly the way people are inconsistent. On every measure anyone bothered to publish, it is fairer. Adams sends good scotch to your office with four handwritten words on the card: 'I was wrong. Sorry.'

choices.text: Drink the scotch with Park
choices.consequence: You open it in chambers with a judge who retires in June, and the two of you argue about what fairness actually measures until the cleaners arrive.

choices.text: Save the scotch for Sara's college graduation
choices.consequence: You put it at the back of a filing cabinet with a sticky note naming a date five years out. It's a bet on a person, and you like the odds.

nodes.text: She walks out through a lobby she had stopped imagining an exit from, and the light on the steps is ordinary and enormous. Marisol films it, because Marisol films everything, and this time nobody tells her to stop. Down the block the aunt is ordering for nine people at a place with laminated menus. The lawyer in you wants the microphones. The rest of you wants to be at that table.

choices.text: Go to the press conference
choices.consequence: You take the microphones, because the next Sara has no lawyer yet and stories are how she gets one. Lunch goes cold in a bag on your desk.

choices.text: Go to the burrito
choices.consequence: You skip the cameras and eat at a folding table with her family while the aunt keeps refilling your plate. The story runs without you. Fine.

nodes.text: She finishes high school a year late and college on time, then law school on a scholarship named for somebody who would have hated the reason she qualified. She is a prosecutor now, and a careful one — she reads every model output twice and makes her juniors explain the features aloud. In your last year practicing she files a brief citing your appeal twice. The signature block reads: your client, your friend.

The judicial council inquiry runs four years, produces a document nobody outside the field will ever read, and terminates three state contracts. The vendor pivots to underwriting, where nobody has a right to counsel and nobody is watching. You end up teaching a seminar called How to Cross-Examine a Black Box. It fills in nine minutes every spring, which is either encouraging or the most depressing fact of your professional life.

Law students learn it as People v. M., because the court anonymized her at your request and she never once asked to be un-anonymized. Three thousand words in a casebook, a standard for auditing an automated finder of fact, and a footnote on inter-rater reliability that ruined one company. She's fine with the initial. Years later she tells you she never wanted to be famous. She wanted to be outside.
nodes.sceneTitle: The Case That Made the Law
nodes.endingTitle: The Case That Made the Law

nodes.text: She goes home to a street with no reporters on it and takes a job at a garden center. You go home tired in a way sleep doesn't fix. Park starts sleeping again. Adams retires early and coaches something. And somewhere in a training run your appeal becomes a document a newer model reads, and the next version does a fraction less harm to somebody who will never learn your name. Enough, you decide. Most days.
